title: Trees and heaps
summary: Maintain the heap invariant with array indexes, and explain why insertion order can turn a binary search tree into a linked list.

scenario.briefing: The campus scheduler keeps deadlines in a min-heap and an index in a binary search tree. A bulk import inserted deadlines in ascending order and the tree became a chain; a hand-written heap update also placed a child before its parent. Implement the heap repair paths and review the tree shape before the import ships.

hints: A new heap value starts at the end of the array and swaps with its parent while it is smaller.

Extract the root, pop the last value, put it at index 0, and bubble down.
Stop bubbling down when neither child is smaller than the current value.

misconceptions.description: Inserting sorted values into an unbalanced search tree.
misconceptions.feedback: Sorted insertion produces a linked chain with linear search. A balanced tree or a different structure is required.

misconceptions.description: Comparing siblings instead of parent and child in a heap.
misconceptions.testDescription: Parent and child indexes follow the array heap layout.
misconceptions.feedback: A heap orders each parent against its children. Sibling order is irrelevant.

misconceptions.description: Scanning the whole heap to find the next value.
misconceptions.testDescription: Extract moves the last value to the root and bubbles it down.
misconceptions.feedback: Extract replaces the root with the last value and repairs downward, keeping the operation logarithmic.

sections.title: A binary search tree orders by key
sections.body: For every node, keys in the left subtree are smaller and keys in the right subtree are larger. Search, insert, and delete follow one path from the root, so their cost is the height of the tree, not the number of nodes.

sections.title: Insertion order decides the height
sections.body: Ascending keys make every new node the right child, so the tree becomes a chain of height n - 1 and search degrades to O(n). A self-balancing tree or a median-first insertion order keeps the height logarithmic, which is why the same key set can have very different costs.

sections.title: A heap orders parents, not subtrees
sections.body: A min-heap requires every parent to be no larger than its children, but it does not order the left child against the right child. The array layout puts the parent at (i - 1) / 2 and the children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.

sections.title: Repair one path per operation
sections.body: Insert bubbles up; extract replaces the root with the last value and bubbles down. Each swap moves one level, so both operations are O(log n). A full scan is O(n) and is not a heap repair.

vocabulary.definition: A binary tree where every left descendant is smaller and every right descendant is larger than the node.
The parent-child rule that makes the root the minimum or maximum; it does not order siblings.
The number of edges on the longest path from the root to a leaf.
A tree whose height stays logarithmic in the number of nodes.
The repair that swaps a value toward the leaves until the heap order holds.

steps.title: Implement a binary min-heap
steps.prompt: Edit trees.ts. Store the heap in an array, bubble a new value up after insert, move the last value to the root and bubble it down after extractMin, and keep parent and child indexes consistent.

tests.description: Insert appends the value and bubbles it up from the last index.
Extract moves the last value to the root and bubbles it down.
Parent and child indexes follow the array heap layout.
Both repair loops stop when the heap order holds.

hints: Insert at the next free index, then restore heap order upward.
Extract by replacing the root with the last value, then bubble down.
Compare a parent at i with children at 2i+1 and 2i+2.
Stop each repair loop as soon as the parent-child order holds.

findings.label: Every key after 5 is inserted as the right child of the previous key, so the tree has height 5 for 6 keys.
Search stays O(log n) because the tree satisfies the binary search tree invariant.
The final height depends on insertion order, not only on the set of keys.
A balanced insertion order or a self-balancing tree would bound the height.
The tree is balanced because every node has at most two children.

verdicts.label: Block the change until the tree shape or the insertion strategy is fixed.
The code only needs formatting changes.
Ship it; a binary search tree is always logarithmic.

steps.explanation: The insert function preserves the BST invariant, but ascending keys create a right spine. Search and insert then walk O(n) nodes. The shape must be bounded by a balanced tree or a different insertion order before this is used for deadlines.
